edges.effect_quant: In a 3-year cohort of 575 normoglycemic Japanese men, adjusted year-3 HOMA-IR was 1.24 in the highest ferritin tertile and 1.22 in the middle tertile versus 1.07 in the lowest tertile (p=0.009); in 226 obese adults, serum ferritin remained independently associated with elevated adipose insulin resistance (OR 1.004, 95% CI 1.000-1.009).
edges.population: adults without hemochromatosis, including normoglycemic men and people with obesity or metabolic risk factors
edges.mechanism: Ferritin reflects higher body iron stores and can rise alongside low-grade inflammation, hepatic steatosis, and adipose dysfunction. Excess iron may worsen oxidative stress, lipolysis, and hepatic and peripheral insulin signaling, which can nudge glucose metabolism toward higher fasting insulin and higher HOMA-IR.
edges.summary: Higher ferritin tracks with more insulin resistance across several adult cohorts, and prospective data suggest the signal is not purely cross-sectional. The effect is modest and confounded by obesity and liver injury, but the overall direction is consistently unfavorable.
edges.caveats: Ferritin is not a pure iron-overload marker because it also rises with inflammation, fatty liver, and alcohol use. Most evidence is observational, so residual confounding remains possible and ferritin may function partly as a risk marker rather than a causal driver.
